fixes.explanation: Asaph says God summons the earth from where the sun rises to where it sets. That stretches from one horizon to the other, friend. No corner of the map is left out of that reach. When the Mighty One calls, it's a big call.

Not quite. Asaph says the opposite: "Our God approaches and will not be silent!" Then he adds that consuming fire precedes Him and a tempest rages around Him. That is no tiptoeing. I'd say that's an arrival you can't miss.

Yes! Asaph says God summons the heavens above and the earth "…that He may judge His people…" The call has a purpose, and the text tells us what it is. God is the Judge, and His people are the ones He judges.
Yes, friend. Asaph says, "And the heavens proclaim His righteousness, for God Himself is Judge." The heavens are doing the announcing. Then the psalm says Selah, right there in the song.

There it is! God says, "…for every beast of the forest is Mine—the cattle on a thousand hills." That's His reason for having no need for a bull from their stall or goats from their pens (Psalm 50:9). The whole forest and a thousand hills of cattle are already His. He doesn't need their animals.
Not quite, friend. God has the cattle on a thousand hills, so a bigger herd wouldn't add anything for Him. What He says is, "Sacrifice a thank offering to God…" That's the offering He names here.

Yes. God says, "You sit and malign your brother; you slander your own mother’s son." The one being slandered is their brother, their mother's son. Slandering a stranger is bad enough, and this one is family.

That's it. God says, "You have done these things, and I kept silent; you thought I was just like you." They thought He was the same as they were. I bet that thought felt comfortable for a while. Then comes, "But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face."
